A fixed-capacity buffer that is read oldest first: writes fail when it is full, reads fail when it is empty, and an overwrite drops the oldest item to make room.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/circular-buffer) (MIT). Listed under [Collections & Algorithms](/examples/?subject=collections-and-algorithms).

```nomi-run
// FILE: circular_buffer.nomi
/// A buffer of at most `capacity` items, read oldest first. It is a value:
/// each operation answers the buffer after it.
pub opaque struct Buffer<T> {
    capacity: Int
    items: List<T>
}

/// Why an operation cannot be done.
pub enum Error {
    Full
    Empty
}

impl Buffer<T> {
    /// An empty buffer that holds at most `capacity` items.
    pub fn new(capacity: Int) -> Buffer<T> {
        #Buffer{capacity, items: []}
    }

    /// `buffer` with `item` after its newest, or `Full` when it holds
    /// `capacity` items already.
    pub fn write(buffer: Buffer<T>, item: T) -> Result<Buffer<T>, Error> {
        if Buffer.full?(buffer) {
            Err(.Full)
        } else {
            Ok(#{..buffer, items: List.concat(buffer.items, [item])})
        }
    }

    /// `buffer` with `item` after its newest, dropping the oldest item first
    /// when it is full.
    pub fn overwrite(buffer: Buffer<T>, item: T) -> Buffer<T> {
        kept = if Buffer.full?(buffer) {
            Iter.drop(buffer.items, 1) |> Iter.to_list()
        } else {
            buffer.items
        }

        #{..buffer, items: List.concat(kept, [item])}
    }

    /// The oldest item and the buffer without it, or `Empty`.
    pub fn read(buffer: Buffer<T>) -> Result<#(T, Buffer<T>), Error> {
        case buffer.items {
            [oldest, ..rest] -> Ok(#(oldest, #{..buffer, items: rest}))
            [] -> Err(.Empty)
        }
    }

    /// `buffer` with no items, at the same capacity.
    pub fn clear(buffer: Buffer<T>) -> Buffer<T> {
        #{..buffer, items: []}
    }

    fn full?(buffer: Buffer<T>) -> Bool {
        Iter.count(buffer.items) == buffer.capacity
    }
}

// FILE: circular_buffer_test.nomi
import circular_buffer.Buffer

/// One canonical operation and what it should do: a write that succeeds or
/// fails, a read of a given item or one that fails, a clear, an overwrite.
enum Step {
    Write Int
    WriteFails Int
    Read Int
    ReadFails
    Clear
    Overwrite Int
}

derive Equatable for Step

/// Runs each step's operation on a buffer of `capacity`, in turn, and
/// answers the steps as they happened. A run that does what every step says
/// answers the steps it was given.
fn replay(capacity: Int, steps: List<Step>) -> List<Step> {
    #(happened, _buffer) =
        steps
        |> Iter.map_reduce(fn buffer = Buffer.new(capacity), step -> {
            case step {
                .Write(item) or .WriteFails(item) -> {
                    case Buffer.write(buffer, item) {
                        Ok(written) -> #(Step.Write(item), written)
                        Err(_) -> #(Step.WriteFails(item), buffer)
                    }
                }

                .Read(_) or .ReadFails -> {
                    case Buffer.read(buffer) {
                        Ok(#(item, rest)) -> #(Step.Read(item), rest)
                        Err(_) -> #(Step.ReadFails, buffer)
                    }
                }

                .Clear ->
                    #(Step.Clear, Buffer.clear(buffer))

                .Overwrite(item) ->
                    #(Step.Overwrite(item), Buffer.overwrite(buffer, item))
            }
        })

    happened
}

test "circular buffer" {
    cases = [
        #("reading empty buffer should fail", 1, [Step.ReadFails]),
        #("can read an item just written", 1, [.Write(1), .Read(1)]),
        #("each item may only be read once", 1, [.Write(1), .Read(1), .ReadFails]),
        #(
            "items are read in the order they are written",
            2,
            [.Write(1), .Write(2), .Read(1), .Read(2)],
        ),
        #("full buffer can't be written to", 1, [.Write(1), .WriteFails(2)]),
        #(
            "a read frees up capacity for another write",
            1,
            [.Write(1), .Read(1), .Write(2), .Read(2)],
        ),
        #(
            "read position is maintained even across multiple writes",
            3,
            [.Write(1), .Write(2), .Read(1), .Write(3), .Read(2), .Read(3)],
        ),
        #("items cleared out of buffer can't be read", 1, [.Write(1), .Clear, .ReadFails]),
        #("clear frees up capacity for another write", 1, [.Write(1), .Clear, .Write(2), .Read(2)]),
        #("clear does nothing on empty buffer", 1, [.Clear, .Write(1), .Read(1)]),
        #(
            "overwrite acts like write on non-full buffer",
            2,
            [.Write(1), .Overwrite(2), .Read(1), .Read(2)],
        ),
        #(
            "overwrite replaces the oldest item on full buffer",
            2,
            [.Write(1), .Write(2), .Overwrite(3), .Read(2), .Read(3)],
        ),
        #(
            "overwrite replaces the oldest item remaining in buffer following a read",
            3,
            [
                .Write(1),
                .Write(2),
                .Write(3),
                .Read(1),
                .Write(4),
                .Overwrite(5),
                .Read(3),
                .Read(4),
                .Read(5),
            ],
        ),
        #(
            "initial clear does not affect wrapping around",
            2,
            [
                .Clear,
                .Write(1),
                .Write(2),
                .Overwrite(3),
                .Overwrite(4),
                .Read(3),
                .Read(4),
                .ReadFails,
            ],
        ),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, capacity, steps), description {
        assert replay(capacity, steps) == steps
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- `Buffer<T>` is a value, an opaque struct of its capacity and its items oldest first. Each operation answers the buffer after it: `write` a `Result<Buffer<T>, Error>`, `read` a `Result<#(T, Buffer<T>), Error>` with the item and the rest, and `clear` and `overwrite` a `Buffer<T>`, since they cannot fail. There is no array and no read or write position to wrap around: the items are a `List`, and the ring is what the operations promise, not how the items are stored.
- The errors are an `Error` enum, `Full` and `Empty`.
- The operations are functions of `impl Buffer<T>`, called `Buffer.write(buffer, 1)` after `import circular_buffer.Buffer`. Each names the block's `T` in its signature and declares no type parameter of its own, so a call takes `T` from its buffer, or, for `Buffer.new(capacity)`, from the type the result is expected to have. `full?` is private to the block.
- The canonical cases are lists of operations, each with whether it should succeed. The test file turns each into a `Step` (`Write(1)`, `WriteFails(2)`, `Read(1)`, `ReadFails`, `Clear`, `Overwrite(3)`), and `replay` runs the steps on a buffer and answers the steps as they happened. A buffer that behaves answers the steps it was given, so each row asserts `replay(capacity, steps) == steps`, and a failure shows the list with the step that went another way.
- `replay` is one `Iter.map_reduce` whose state is the buffer and whose output is each step as it happened. A failed write or read keeps the buffer as it was.
- The 14 canonical cases are one `subtests` table named by the description column. The first row qualifies its first step, `Step.Write(1)`, and the steps after it are bare.
